sentences.text: Owning something means you control it – not that you control it until the seller changes their mind.
I know that sounds obvious.
It's apparently not.

When you buy a phone, a tractor, a car, or a smart thermostat, you hand over money and receive a physical object – and you also receive a relationship with the company that made it, one with terms you didn't negotiate and can't opt out of.
The company can push a software update and remove features you paid for.

claims.claim: A device maker can push a software update and remove features the buyer paid for.
claims.request_basis: its maker can disable features after sale

sentences.text: It can decide, remotely and unilaterally, that what you bought last year isn't what you'll have next year.
That's not a purchase.
That's a lease with the audacity to charge you full price up front.
Think about what we mean when we say someone owns a building.
The new owner can renovate it, neglect it, or sell it to someone else – none of that is the previous owner's business, because the transfer was complete.
Ownership, in the traditional sense, means the seller's interest ends at the point of sale.

What we've got now is something different: a model where the manufacturer retains silent equity in every device they've ever shipped (redeemable at any time through a firmware update, at their discretion and for their reasons).
I think we'd have a very specific word for this arrangement if we encountered it in real estate.
We'd call it fraud.
What does it actually look like when a company exercises this residual control?
You buy a printer that works with third-party ink; a firmware update makes it stop.
You buy a car with heated seats; the manufacturer decides that feature is now a monthly subscription, eighteen months after you drove it off the lot.
You buy a robot vacuum, the company gets acquired, the servers go dark, and now you've got a very expensive hockey puck.
The question the industry never wants to answer is: when exactly did you agree that the purchase price bought them an ongoing veto over how you use the thing you own?
We didn't agree to that, and we shouldn't pretend the existing legal frameworks cover it.

The argument you'll hear from manufacturers is usually wrapped in language about 'security updates' and 'service continuity' – and I don't think that's complete bullshit, but it is a remarkably convenient alibi for a straightforward power grab.
A security patch that happens to delete features you paid for isn't a security patch.
It's renegotiating the sale after the fact, with you holding no cards.
We have warranty law, implied covenants of merchantability, consumer protection statutes – none of it was designed for a world where the seller keeps their hands on the thing indefinitely.
The fix isn't hard to describe (it's hard to pass, because the companies lobbying against it have a great deal of money, but that's a different problem).
Require that any feature present at point of sale remain functional for the device's reasonable useful life, or require a full refund when it's stripped.
Mandate disclosure of every cloud dependency (including the services that can be sunset without notice) before purchase, not buried in paragraph forty-seven of a EULA nobody reads.
And I'd add this: if a company wants the right to keep modifying what you bought after you bought it, make them lease it.
Stop letting them call it a sale.
Ownership is not a subscription.
Until we treat post-sale feature removal as what it actually is – a taking, and a fairly brazen one – we're all just renting from companies that already collected the purchase price.
